In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms by which the thymus determines the repertoire of antigen‐specific T lymphocytes.
the role of the thymus, and the influence of thymic genotype, on the development and expression of T cell responsiveness.
the role of the thymus and the MHC in the development of the immune response to a variety of antigens, in particular those controlled by the Ir genes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
thymic genotype determines the repertoire of T cells available for sensitization, but that the repertoire can be restricted by antigen‐pulsing of Mph.
the thymus genotype influences the acquisition of responsiveness in DTH.
the T cell repertoire is restricted by the thymus, but that the thymus is influenced by the Mph.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Ir genes control the ability of the Mph to present antigen and that the thymus is the site where T cells become responsive to antigen presented in association with Mph.
the thymus is the major site of restriction in the immune system.

Ir gene products are required for the generation of a T cell population capable of responding to the appropriate antigen and that the T cell population generated in the thymus is not necessarily the same as that generated in the periphery.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the T cell receptor (TCR) is a key player in the process of antigen recognition and T cell activation, and that it is a key player that is not fixed but rather is highly variable.
the thymus plays a critical role in T‐cell development and differentiation.
the thymus is not just a place where T cells develop.
